Fetal growth is at the 70th percentile. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Continue diet and exercise, and review the log in 4 weeks
Plan induction of labour at 34 weeks
items.explanationHtml:
The targets are fasting below 95 mg/dL and 1-hour postprandial below 140 mg/dL. Her postprandial values meet the target, but every fasting value is above it despite nutrition therapy. Insulin is preferred when GDM needs medication, because it does not cross the placenta and can be titrated precisely. Bedtime intermediate-acting (NPH) insulin targets fasting hyperglycemia. Antenatal testing is added once she is on medication.

Takeaway: GDM that misses targets on diet: start insulin. Use bedtime NPH for high fasting values and prandial insulin for high postprandial values.

whyNot.B: Persistent fasting hyperglycemia for 2 weeks should be treated now, not reviewed in 4 weeks.
whyNot.C: Glyburide crosses the placenta and is associated with more neonatal hypoglycemia and macrosomia than insulin. It is not preferred.
whyNot.D: Well-controlled GDM on medication is delivered at 39 weeks. Delivery at 34 weeks is not indicated.
whyNot.E: DPP-4 inhibitors are not used to treat GDM.

items.objective: Start insulin for gestational diabetes with persistent fasting hyperglycemia despite nutrition therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks' gestation has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the antenatal clinic waiting room. She had a headache this morning. After the seizure stops, she is turned on her left side and given oxygen, and her airway is clear. Blood pressure is 166/108 mm Hg. Fetal heart rate monitoring shows a bradycardia of 90/min that is beginning to recover. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: CT of the head before any medication
items.explanationHtml:
A new seizure with hypertension at 36 weeks is eclampsia. After the airway is secured and she is turned onto her side, the next step is a magnesium sulfate loading dose (4 to 6 g IV) followed by an infusion, which prevents recurrent seizures better than benzodiazepines or phenytoin. Severe-range blood pressure should be treated next. Fetal bradycardia during and just after the seizure usually recovers as the mother is stabilised, so delivery is planned once she is stable.

Takeaway: Eclampsia: protect the airway, then magnesium sulfate, then control blood pressure, and deliver once the mother is stable.

whyNot.B: Benzodiazepines are used only if seizures continue despite magnesium, or when magnesium is unavailable.
whyNot.C: Phenytoin is less effective than magnesium for preventing recurrent eclamptic seizures.
whyNot.D: Operating before the mother is stabilised adds risk, and the fetal bradycardia is recovering.
whyNot.E: Imaging is for atypical features or focal deficits, and it should not delay magnesium.

items.objective: Give magnesium sulfate as first-line treatment for eclampsia.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 1, at 22 weeks' gestation is Rh(D)-negative. She did not receive anti-D immune globulin after a miscarriage 3 years ago. Her anti-D titer was 1:8 at 12 weeks and is now 1:64. Her partner is the father of all her pregnancies and is homozygous Rh(D)-positive. Ultrasonography shows a normally grown fetus with no ascites or skin edema. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Doppler measurement of middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity
Repeat the antibody titer in 4 weeks
items.explanationHtml:
Her titer has risen above the critical level (usually 1:16), and her homozygous partner means the fetus must be D-positive. The next step is serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity Doppler, every 1 to 2 weeks. Anemic fetal blood is less viscous and cardiac output is higher, so a velocity above 1.5 MoM predicts moderate to severe anemia and leads to cordocentesis with intrauterine transfusion.

Takeaway: At or above the critical anti-D titer, monitor for fetal anemia with MCA peak systolic velocity Doppler. Cordocentesis is for velocities above 1.5 MoM.

whyNot.B: Anti-D immune globulin does nothing once the patient is sensitised.
whyNot.C: Serial titers are used only below the critical titer. Above it, fetal surveillance is needed.
whyNot.D: Delivery at 22 weeks would be previable and is not indicated without evidence of severe anemia.
whyNot.E: Cordocentesis is invasive and is kept for abnormal Doppler findings or hydrops.

items.objective: Use MCA Doppler surveillance once the anti-D titer reaches the critical level.

MeasurementResult

Glucose51 mg/dL (2.8 mmol/L)

Bilirubin, total5.6 mg/dL (96 µmol/L)

Creatinine1.6 mg/dL (141 µmol/L)
Platelets128,000/mm³ (128 × 10⁹/L)
Peripheral smearNo schistocytes
Hepatitis A, B, C serologiesNegative

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Third-trimester liver dysfunction with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy (high INR, low fibrinogen), jaundice and renal injury points to acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Mild or absent hypertension and the absence of hemolysis make HELLP less likely. Management is stabilisation (glucose, blood products) and prompt delivery, and the newborn should be tested for fatty acid oxidation disorders.

Takeaway: Hypoglycemia plus coagulopathy and jaundice in the third trimester suggests acute fatty liver of pregnancy rather than HELLP.

whyNot.B: HELLP needs hemolysis and platelets below 100,000/mm³, and hypoglycemia and early coagulopathy are uncommon.
whyNot.C: Cholestasis of pregnancy causes itching and high bile acids without liver failure, hypoglycemia or coagulopathy.
whyNot.D: TTP causes microangiopathic hemolysis with schistocytes and severe thrombocytopenia, not hepatic failure with hypoglycemia.
whyNot.E: Hyperemesis is a first-trimester condition and does not cause this degree of liver failure at 35 weeks.

items.objective: Distinguish acute fatty liver of pregnancy from HELLP syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman at 8 weeks' gestation has nausea most of the day and vomits two or three times daily. She is keeping fluids down, her weight is stable, and urine ketones are negative. Small frequent meals and ginger have not helped enough. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line drug therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
For nausea and vomiting of pregnancy that persists despite dietary measures, ACOG recommends pyridoxine (vitamin B6), alone or combined with doxylamine, as first-line drug therapy. It is effective and has a strong safety record. Antihistamines, dopamine antagonists and ondansetron are added if symptoms persist. Corticosteroids are kept for refractory hyperemesis and avoided before 10 weeks.

Takeaway: First-line drug therapy for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy is pyridoxine with or without doxylamine.

whyNot.B: Ondansetron is a later option, after weighing a possible small first-trimester risk and the effect on the QT interval.
whyNot.C: Corticosteroids are a last resort for refractory hyperemesis and are avoided before 10 weeks.
whyNot.D: Metoclopramide is a second-line agent with a risk of extrapyramidal effects.
whyNot.E: She is not dehydrated or ketotic, so IV fluids are not needed.

items.objective: Prescribe pyridoxine with or without doxylamine as first-line therapy for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman with monochorionic diamniotic twins has routine ultrasonography at 19 weeks. Twin A has a deepest vertical pocket of 1.2 cm, appears pressed against the uterine wall, and its bladder is not seen during the 60-minute examination. Twin B has a deepest pocket of 9.5 cm and a distended bladder. Umbilical artery and venous Dopplers are normal in both, and neither twin has hydrops. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Referral for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses
Indomethacin to reduce fluid in twin B
items.explanationHtml:
Oligohydramnios in one twin and polyhydramnios in the other, in a monochorionic pair, is twin-twin transfusion syndrome. A donor bladder that cannot be seen, with normal Dopplers, is Quintero stage II. For stages II to IV between 16 and 26 weeks, fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the anastomoses gives better survival and neurologic outcome than amnioreduction.

Takeaway: TTTS stages II to IV at 16 to 26 weeks are treated with fetoscopic laser ablation of the shared vessels.

whyNot.B: Amnioreduction relieves symptoms but does not treat the cause, and its outcomes are worse than laser treatment.
whyNot.C: Delivery at 19 weeks is previable.
whyNot.D: Indomethacin is not a treatment for TTTS and can harm both fetuses.
whyNot.E: TTTS can progress quickly. Monochorionic twins need scans every 2 weeks, and this stage needs treatment now.

items.objective: Refer stage II twin-twin transfusion syndrome for fetoscopic laser therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation, dated by first-trimester ultrasonography, has an estimated fetal weight at the 6th percentile, with a relatively small abdominal circumference. Amniotic fluid is normal, and the anatomy scan at 20 weeks was normal. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. A nonstress test is reactive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Delivery after a course of betamethasone
items.explanationHtml:
An estimated fetal weight below the 10th percentile is fetal growth restriction. Umbilical artery Doppler is the key test, because it distinguishes a fetus with placental insufficiency from one that is constitutionally small, and it sets the surveillance and the timing of delivery. Normal Doppler with an EFW between the 3rd and 10th percentile supports delivery at 38 to 39 weeks. Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow means earlier delivery.

Takeaway: After diagnosing FGR, get umbilical artery Doppler to guide surveillance and delivery timing.

whyNot.B: Delivery at 32 weeks is not indicated without abnormal Doppler or testing.
whyNot.C: Growth scans are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks. Measurement error makes a 1-week interval unhelpful.
whyNot.D: Starting aspirin after FGR is diagnosed does not treat it.
whyNot.E: Bed rest does not improve fetal growth and carries maternal risks.

items.objective: Order umbilical artery Doppler after a diagnosis of fetal growth restriction.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 0, is at 12 weeks' gestation with a viable singleton fetus. Her two previous pregnancies ended at 19 and 20 weeks with painless cervical dilation and bulging membranes, without contractions, bleeding or infection. She had a cervical cone biopsy 6 years ago. Today the cervix is closed. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Cervical cerclage at about 12 to 14 weeks
Placement of a cervical pessary at 24 weeks
items.explanationHtml:
Previous second-trimester losses from painless dilation, without labour or abruption, are the classic history of cervical insufficiency, made more likely by her cone biopsy. A history-indicated cerclage at about 12 to 14 weeks, after confirming a viable fetus without major anomalies, is recommended. Vaginal progesterone is for a short cervix in people without a previous preterm birth, and bed rest does not help.

Takeaway: Previous painless second-trimester losses (cervical insufficiency) call for a history-indicated cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks.

whyNot.B: Vaginal progesterone is for a short cervix found on ultrasound without a history like this one.
whyNot.C: Hydroxyprogesterone caproate was withdrawn from the US market in 2023 because it was not effective.
whyNot.D: Bed rest does not prevent preterm birth and raises the risk of VTE and deconditioning.
whyNot.E: Pessaries have not consistently prevented preterm birth, and 24 weeks is after her previous losses.

items.objective: Place a history-indicated cerclage for cervical insufficiency.
